question: What are the three sources of bleed air for the pneumatic system?

options.text: Engines, APU and ram air inlets
Engines, APU and ground pneumatic source
Engines, packs and recirculation fans
APU, ram air and the ground cart

explanation: The engines are the normal source in flight, the APU is the normal source on the ground, and a ground cart can substitute when the APU is unserviceable.

question: From which compressor stages is engine bleed air taken?

options.text: The 5th and 9th stages
The 2nd and 5th stages
The 9th and 13th stages
The fan and the 5th stage

explanation: Two ports are needed because a single port cannot deliver usable pressure across the whole range of thrust settings and altitudes.

question: When does the high stage valve open?

options.text: When 5th stage pressure is insufficient to meet demand
Whenever the engine is running above idle thrust
Only during engine start and the pushback phase
Whenever the pack switch is selected to HIGH flow

explanation: Low thrust settings and high altitude reduce 5th stage pressure, so the 9th stage is brought in to keep the duct supplied.

question: Why is the lower compressor stage used whenever it can meet the demand?

options.text: Extracting air from a later stage costs more engine performance and fuel
It delivers cleaner air and reduces the risk of duct contamination
It produces noticeably less noise in the cabin at cruise
It is the only stage available above the tropopause in the cruise

explanation: Air taken later in the compressor has already had more work done on it, so bleeding it is a larger penalty on thrust and fuel burn.

question: What is the function of the pre-cooler?

options.text: It removes moisture from the bleed air
It cools the bleed air using engine fan air
It raises bleed pressure before the packs
It filters contaminants out of the bleed air

explanation: Bleed air leaves the compressor far too hot for the ducts and the packs, so fan air is used as the cooling medium.

question: What does the fan air modulating valve control?

options.text: The pack flow rate selected on the pack switch
The position of the ram air inlet doors
The quantity of fan air passed through the pre-cooler
The bleed air pressure delivered to the pneumatic duct

explanation: By modulating the cooling airflow it holds the bleed air temperature downstream of the pre-cooler at the scheduled value.

question: What is the effect of selecting an engine BLEED air switch OFF?

options.text: The engine bleed air valve closes
The pack on that side shuts down immediately
The isolation valve closes automatically
The high stage valve opens to compensate

explanation: Closing the valve isolates that engine from the duct. The pack can still be supplied from the other side if the isolation valve is open.

question: What condition causes the BLEED TRIP OFF light to illuminate?

options.text: Failure of the pack cooling fan
A leak in the wing leading edge
Bleed air overpressure or overtemperature
Loss of the ram air door position signal

explanation: The bleed valve closes automatically to protect the ducts and downstream equipment from damage.

question: What is the function of the TRIP RESET switch?

options.text: It resets the cabin pressure controller to auto
It restores the recirculation fans to normal
It cancels the cabin altitude warning horn
It reopens a tripped valve once the cause has cleared

explanation: The reset only works after the overheat or overpressure condition has gone, so it cannot be used to force a faulty system back on line.

question: What does the DUAL BLEED light warn the crew about?

options.text: Both packs are operating in high flow together
Both engine bleed valves have tripped off
APU bleed and engine bleed are supplying the same duct
The isolation valve has failed in the closed position

explanation: Engine bleed pressure can drive air back towards the APU, so the configuration is corrected to avoid damaging the APU.

question: What are the positions of the isolation valve switch?

options.text: OPEN and CLOSE only
OFF, AUTO and ON
NORM, ALTN and OFF
CLOSE, AUTO and OPEN

explanation: AUTO is the normal selection, leaving the system to connect or separate the two duct sides as the configuration requires.

question: With the isolation valve switch in AUTO, when does the valve open?

options.text: Only when both engine bleed switches are selected off
When a pack switch or a bleed air switch is selected OFF
Whenever the APU is running and supplying the duct
Whenever the flaps are extended for landing

explanation: Losing a source or a user on one side means the two ducts must be joined so the remaining supply can reach both. Verify the exact logic against your operator FCOM.

question: What does the WING-BODY OVERHEAT light indicate?

options.text: A bleed air leak in the duct area of the wing or body
A pack outlet overheat downstream of the valve
An engine anti-ice valve failed in the open position
Overheating of the equipment cooling exhaust duct

explanation: Hot escaping air is detected by sensing elements running alongside the ducts, which is how a leak is found before it damages structure.

question: What is the first consideration after a wing-body overheat indication?

options.text: Isolate the affected bleed source
Increase pack flow to cool the duct
Open the isolation valve to share the flow
Select both packs to HIGH flow

explanation: Shutting off the source removes the hot air feeding the leak. Sharing the flow would spread the problem rather than contain it.

question: What does the duct pressure indicator display?

options.text: Cabin differential pressure in the climb
Left and right pneumatic duct pressure
Pack discharge pressure at the outlet
Ram air pressure at the inlet duct

explanation: The dual indication lets the crew see each side separately and judge whether a source or a valve has failed.

question: Which system is pressurised by bleed air to prevent pump cavitation?

options.text: The fuel tank vent system
The crew oxygen cylinders
The rain repellent system
The hydraulic reservoirs

explanation: Positive pressure on the reservoirs keeps fluid supplied to the pump inlets, especially at altitude.

question: Which of the following is also supplied by bleed air?

options.text: The landing gear extension system
The potable water tank pressurisation
The flight control hydraulic actuators
The passenger oxygen generators

explanation: Pressurising the tank forces water to the galleys and lavatories without a separate pump.

question: Which of these functions depends on the pneumatic system?

options.text: Nose wheel steering
Autobrake operation
Flight control feel
Engine starting

explanation: The starter is air driven, which is why a bleed source is required before an engine can be started.

question: Which ice protection function uses bleed air directly?

options.text: Windshield and window heat
Pitot and static probe heat
Thermal wing and engine anti-ice
Total air temperature probe heat

explanation: Wing and cowl anti-ice are thermal systems fed from the ducts, whereas probe and window heating are electrical.

question: To which side does the APU bleed air valve deliver air?

options.text: The left duct
The right duct
Both ducts equally
The mix manifold

explanation: Air reaches the right side only through the isolation valve, which is why that valve matters during APU operation.

question: Can the APU supply both packs on the ground?

options.text: No, only one pack at a time
Only if both engines are running
Yes, with the isolation valve open
Only with the packs in HIGH flow

explanation: This is the normal ground configuration for cooling the cabin before engine start.

question: What limits the use of APU bleed air in flight?

options.text: The number of engines running at the time
The position of the trailing edge flaps
The cabin differential pressure in the climb
A maximum altitude for bleed extraction

explanation: APU bleed performance falls off with altitude, so its use in flight is restricted by an altitude limit. Verify the figure against your operator FCOM.

question: What is a ground pneumatic source normally used for?

options.text: Charging the hydraulic accumulators and pressurising the reservoirs
Pressurising the cabin on the ground during turnaround
Supplying the equipment cooling fans in hot conditions
Supplying the packs and starting an engine when the APU is unavailable

explanation: It substitutes for the APU as a source of duct pressure, which is why dispatch with an inoperative APU depends on its availability.

question: What is the consequence of having no bleed air source available in flight?

options.text: There is no pack output and therefore no pressurisation
Only the flight deck remains air conditioned
The packs run on ram air alone in the cruise
The cabin pressurises from the recirculation fans

explanation: Conditioned air comes only from the packs, which are supplied by bleed air, so the loss of bleed is also the loss of pressurisation.

question: How many air conditioning packs are installed?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: One pack on each side, normally fed from the duct on its own side, which preserves independence between the two systems.

question: What are the positions of the pack switch?

options.text: OFF, NORM and MAX
OFF, LOW and HIGH
AUTO, MAN and OFF
OFF, AUTO and HIGH

explanation: AUTO lets the system schedule the flow, while HIGH is a manual selection for extra cooling or heating capacity.

question: With the pack switch in AUTO, what causes a pack to change to high flow automatically?

options.text: The other pack not operating
Selection of engine anti-ice
Cabin altitude above 8000 ft
Extension of the landing gear

explanation: A single pack must move more air to condition the whole cabin, so the system compensates automatically for the loss of the other one.

question: What does an illuminated PACK light indicate?

options.text: The pack is operating continuously in high flow
The pack has tripped off because of an overheat
Ram air is being used to cool the pack
The pack switch has been left in AUTO

explanation: The pack shuts itself down to prevent damage, and can be reset with the trip reset switch once it has cooled.

question: Which machine is at the heart of each pack?

options.text: An air cycle machine with a compressor and a turbine
A vapour cycle refrigeration compressor and condenser
A centrifugal water separator and condenser
A rotary bleed air pressure multiplier

explanation: Air is compressed, cooled, then expanded through the turbine, and the work extracted in the turbine is what produces the temperature drop.

question: What is used as the cooling medium in the pack heat exchangers?

options.text: Fan air
Fuel
Ram air
Cabin air

explanation: Outside air passing through the ram air circuit carries away the heat of compression before the air is expanded.

question: How is cooling airflow obtained through the heat exchangers on the ground?

options.text: No cooling is available until the airplane starts moving forward
The recirculation fans are reversed to draw air in
The air cycle machine fan draws air through the ram air circuit
The equipment cooling exhaust fan is used instead

explanation: With no forward speed there is no ram effect, so the fan provides the airflow the heat exchangers need.

question: What does the RAM DOOR FULL OPEN light indicate?

options.text: A failure of the ram air door actuator to drive the door closed in flight
Ram air is being used instead of pack output to cool the cabin
The pack has reverted to manual temperature control by the crew
The ram air door is fully open, which is normal on the ground and at low speed

explanation: At low speed the door opens fully to get enough cooling airflow, so the light is a normal indication in that regime.

question: Why is moisture removed from the conditioned air before it reaches the cabin?

options.text: To reduce the load on the recirculation fans
To prevent fogging and the formation of ice in the system
To keep the cabin humidity above the minimum required
To protect the trim air valves from corrosion

explanation: Cooling the air condenses the water it carries, and that water would otherwise freeze in the cold sections and blow into the cabin as fog.

question: What is the function of the mix manifold?

options.text: It combines left and right bleed air ahead of both packs
It blends ram air with bleed air for temperature control
It mixes trim air with cabin exhaust air before it is discharged
It mixes pack output with recirculated cabin air before distribution

explanation: Mixing allows a comfortable cabin flow to be maintained while taking less air from the engines.

question: How many recirculation fans are installed on the 737-800?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: The longer fuselage needs more recirculation capacity than the shorter variants. Verify the fit against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the main operational benefit of recirculating cabin air?

options.text: It improves cabin humidity and reduces dryness
It increases the maximum cabin differential pressure
It allows the packs to be operated at higher temperatures
It reduces the bleed air demand and therefore fuel burn

explanation: Every kilogram of air not taken from the engines is thrust and fuel retained, which is why recirculation is used whenever it is available.

question: How is recirculated air treated before it returns to the mix manifold?

options.text: It is reheated by trim air
It passes through filters
It is passed through the pack turbine
It is dried in the water separator

explanation: Filtration removes particles and contaminants, which is what makes reusing cabin air acceptable.

question: How is trim air used in temperature control?

options.text: Cold pack air is bypassed around the mix manifold into the cabin
Hot bleed air is added downstream of the packs to warm an individual zone
Ram air is admitted directly into the cabin through the zone valve
Recirculated air is diverted to the flight deck zone only

explanation: The packs supply air at the temperature required by the coldest zone, and each warmer zone is then trimmed up individually.

question: What does a ZONE TEMP light indicate?

options.text: That the zone temperature selector is in the manual position
That the zone has reached the selected temperature setting
Failure of a recirculation fan serving that zone
A duct overheat in that zone, with the trim air valve closing

explanation: Closing the trim air valve removes the source of the hot air, which protects the duct and the cabin.

question: How is the flight deck temperature controlled relative to the cabin?

options.text: It shares the setting used for the forward cabin
It has its own independently selected zone
It is fixed by the pack temperature controller
It follows the forward cabin zone automatically

explanation: The flight deck has a very different heat load from avionics, sunlight and a small occupied volume, so it needs separate control.

question: Which pack normally supplies conditioned air to the flight deck?

options.text: The right pack
The left pack
Both packs equally
Whichever is in high flow

explanation: Knowing the normal distribution matters when a pack fails or when smoke in the flight deck has to be traced to a source.

question: From where are the individual overhead air outlets supplied?

options.text: Directly from the left pack
From the ram air inlet
From the recirculation system
From the trim air manifold

explanation: They provide local airflow rather than conditioned pack air, which is why the air from them is close to cabin temperature.

question: How is the electronic equipment cooled?

options.text: By a dedicated vapour cycle refrigeration unit
By pack air ducted directly to each individual equipment rack
By supply and exhaust fans drawing air across the equipment
By ram air alone through a dedicated cooling inlet

explanation: Continuous forced airflow is required because the avionics generate heat whenever they are powered.

question: What are the selections available for the equipment cooling fans?

options.text: NORMAL and ALTERNATE
LOW and HIGH
AUTO and MANUAL
ON and STANDBY

explanation: A second fan is available on each of the supply and exhaust sides, so a single fan failure does not stop the cooling.

question: What does an equipment cooling OFF light indicate?

options.text: That the fan switch has been left in ALTERNATE
That the equipment cooling exhaust air is too cold
That there is insufficient airflow from the selected fan
That the smoke detector in the exhaust has been tested

explanation: Loss of airflow is sensed directly, and the response is to select the alternate fan and confirm the flow is restored.

question: Why is the equipment cooling exhaust monitored for smoke?

options.text: Because smoke there is an early indication of an electrical or avionics fire
To protect the pack heat exchangers from soot contamination
To detect a bleed air leak in the equipment bay beneath the flight deck
To confirm when the equipment cooling filters need replacement

explanation: All the cooling air passes through the exhaust path, so it is the single place where an avionics fire shows itself first.

question: What is the operational consequence of losing both packs in flight?

options.text: A descent is required because pressurisation is lost
The cabin is cooled by ram air alone until landing
The recirculation fans maintain cabin pressure alone
The APU restores pressurisation above its bleed limit

explanation: Without pack output the cabin altitude climbs towards the airplane altitude, so the only remedy is to descend.

question: How many outflow valves control cabin pressure?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: A single valve is sufficient because cabin pressure is set by how much air is allowed to leave, not by the number of valves.

question: Where is the outflow valve located?

options.text: In the wing root fairing
Behind the forward cargo compartment
In the tail cone below the APU
In the lower aft fuselage

explanation: Positioning it aft and low uses the natural front to back airflow through the cabin and keeps the discharge clear of the structure.

question: How is the outflow valve driven in the manual mode?

options.text: By the same AC motor as in auto
By differential pressure alone
By a pneumatic actuator
By a separate DC motor

explanation: An independent motor on a different power source is what allows manual control to survive the failures that disable the automatic modes.

question: What are the three cabin pressurisation modes?

options.text: AUTO, ALTN and MAN
AUTO, NORM and STBY
NORM, ALTN and OFF
AUTO, SEMI and MAN

explanation: AUTO is normal, ALTN uses the second controller, and MAN gives the crew direct control of valve position.

question: Why are two automatic cabin pressure controllers fitted?

options.text: To control the forward and aft cabin zones separately
To allow simultaneous control of both outflow valves
So that a failure of one can be covered by selecting the other
To provide separate control for the climb and the descent

explanation: Redundancy in the controller keeps automatic operation available after a single failure, without going to manual control.

question: Which of the following will illuminate the AUTO FAIL light?

options.text: Selection of the manual mode
Opening of the isolation valve
Loss of one recirculation fan
A failure of the controller in use

explanation: The light draws attention to the loss of automatic control so the crew can transfer to the alternate system.

question: What is the normal crew response to an AUTO FAIL indication?

options.text: Select the manual mode immediately
Switch both packs to HIGH
Select the alternate mode
Close the outflow valve manually

explanation: The alternate controller is the next level of automation and is tried before accepting the workload of manual control.

question: What is the purpose of the FLT ALT selector?

options.text: To set the planned cruise altitude so the cabin can be scheduled
To set the maximum cabin altitude allowed in the cruise
To set the altitude at which the packs revert to high flow
To set the altitude for automatic APU shutdown in flight

explanation: The controller needs to know the cruise level to plan a smooth cabin climb rather than reacting to the airplane altitude alone.

question: What is set on the LAND ALT selector?

options.text: The cabin altitude at which the warning horn sounds
The altitude for the start of the cabin descent
The minimum cabin altitude in the cruise
The elevation of the destination airport

explanation: Scheduling the cabin towards field elevation means the cabin and the airplane arrive at the same pressure together.

question: What does the OFF SCHED DESCENT light indicate?

options.text: The cabin is descending faster than the rate the controller selected
The outflow valve has failed in the descent schedule
The landing altitude has been set below field elevation
A descent has been started before reaching the selected cruise altitude

explanation: The controller has to abandon its planned schedule and recalculate, and the light tells the crew why the cabin behaviour has changed.

question: At what cabin altitude does the cabin altitude warning horn sound?
explanation: The warning is set where useful consciousness begins to be affected. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the approximate maximum normal cabin differential pressure?

options.text: 6.5 psi
7.45 psi
8.65 psi
9.8 psi

explanation: The limit is a structural one set by the fuselage design. Verify the exact figure against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the function of the positive pressure relief valves?

options.text: To vent the cabin during an emergency descent to sea level
To equalise pressure across the flight deck door in a decompression
To prevent the differential pressure from exceeding the structural limit
To relieve duct pressure after a bleed air valve trips off

explanation: They act mechanically and independently of the controllers, so an outflow valve stuck closed cannot overpressurise the fuselage.

question: What does the negative pressure relief protect against?

options.text: Cabin pressure exceeding the maximum differential
Loss of cabin pressure during a rapid descent
Outside pressure becoming higher than cabin pressure
An excessive cabin rate of climb in the climb

explanation: The structure is designed to be pushed outward, not inward, and a rapid descent with the cabin sealed could otherwise reverse the load.

question: How is cabin altitude actually controlled?

options.text: By varying the amount of air leaving through the outflow valve
By varying the pack flow delivered into the cabin
By modulating the speed of both recirculation fans together
By varying the bleed air pressure at the ducts

explanation: Inflow from the packs is essentially constant, so it is the outflow that sets the cabin pressure at any moment.

question: What is the normal position of the outflow valve on the ground?

options.text: Fully closed
Partly modulating
As left at touchdown
Fully open

explanation: An open valve guarantees there is no residual differential, which is what allows the doors to be opened safely.

question: What is the approximate maximum normal cabin rate of climb in the automatic mode?

options.text: About 300 ft per minute
About 500 ft per minute
About 1000 ft per minute
About 2000 ft per minute

explanation: The rate is chosen for passenger comfort and ear clearance rather than for system capability. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the risk of setting a landing altitude significantly higher than the actual field elevation?

options.text: The cabin will climb too rapidly in the descent
The outflow valve will close at top of descent
The cabin may still be pressurised at touchdown
The AUTO FAIL light will illuminate in the cruise

explanation: A residual differential at the gate makes the doors dangerous to open, which is why the landing altitude setting is verified during the approach preparation.

question: What does the crew monitor when operating in the manual pressurisation mode?

options.text: Duct pressure and pack outlet temperature
Cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential pressure
Ram air door position and pack flow rate
Zone temperatures and trim air valve position

explanation: In manual mode nothing schedules the cabin for the crew, so the three indications are the only feedback on what the valve movement is achieving.

question: Why does the cabin not pressurise during ground operations with the packs running?

options.text: The packs deliver too little flow on the ground
The recirculation fans vent the cabin overboard
The outflow valve is commanded open
The relief valves are held open by ground sensing

explanation: Holding the valve open lets all the pack air pass straight out, so the cabin stays at field pressure while still being ventilated.
